newsitem.title: UK: More oil refineries to close in Europe than in US.
newsitem.headline: More oil refineries to close in Europe than in US.

text.p: Oil companies hit by poor refining margins will be forced to shut more refineries in Europe than in the United States where a slew of recent oil company alliances is likely to slash overheads, analysts said.

"I would be surprised if there were not two or three more closures in Europe by the end of 1998 and I don't believe it stops there either," said Jeremy Hudson, an energy analyst at Salomon Brothers in London. "I think this phase will last five to 10 years."
"There will be some closures in the U.S. but not as much as in Europe."

According to Mathieu Zajdela, head of studies at consultants Enerfinance in Paris, closure plans announced so far in Europe are timid to date and will not dent overcapacity by anything like the 10 percent reduction many refiners believe is needed.
"There have been a lot of announcements but when you look at the details it is much less clear," he said.
Shell has said it wants to roughly halve capacity, starting in 1998, at its 127,000 bpd Berre refinery in southern France.
Kuwait Petroleum's 60,000 bpd refinery in Denmark and Chevron's 115,000 bpd Pembroke plant are due to be axed.

British Petroleum Co Plc will lose 70,000 barrels per day when it shuts the Nerefco section of the Pernis refinery in Rotterdam, while capacity is to be slashed by 60,000 bpd at Exxon's plant in Karlsruhe, Germany.
Adding these on to possible shut-ins still under discussion, total closures could add up to 600,000 bpd.

But upgrading work at the Beta refinery in Germany will add some 30,000 bpd of throughput, modernisation at the Leuna refinery in Germany will add another 70,000 bpd and upgrades at Holborn another 20,000 bpd.
And Zajdela said ongoing debottlenecking across Western Europe will raise capacity perhaps by 0.5 to one percent of its 12 million bpd capacity. This is equivalent to 60-120,000 bpd.
Taking only the confirmed closures and capacity increases into account, the net result may be a capacity reduction in Europe of as little as 100,000-150,00 bpd.
"As you can see, we are very far from the 10 percent cutback that some have been calling for," Zajdela said.
Hudson said that recent U.S. oil company alliances would help strip out overheads but would not necessarily lead to large refinery closures.
Texaco and Shell said last week they would combine their U.S. downstream operations in a $10 billion merger, while Valero Energy Corp has bought Salomon Inc's Basis Refining unit for $485 million.
Independents like Tosco Corp, too, have been snapping up refining assets which are at bargain-basement prices because of the current climate of bad refining margins.
"Specialist refining companies are increasingly becoming owners and the integrated companies are getting out," he said.

Energy consultant Cindy Poynter of Bonnner and Moore in Germany said it would be easier to close refineries in Europe than in the United States, which imports refined products, and where refiners are currently putting crude oil through their refineries at well over 90 percent of capacity.
"You pay higher prices for imports. They will streamline operations (in the U.S.) although I am not sure they will be shutting in so much capacity."

Europe's position as a swing refining centre, however - gas oil tends to sail eastwards from the Mediterranean while northwest European refiners often sell gasoline to the U.S. - reflects structural overcapacity and means closures in Europe will be deeper, she added.
Hudson also said that while improving global margins, powered by strong demand growth in Asia, would help prevent U.S. refiners from closing, the picture would be different in Europe.
"Although I think margins are going to go up over the next few years they are not likely to go up enough to transform the economics of these (European) projects.
"The closure pressure will still be there early into the next decade," he said. Tightening European environmental legislation was expected to be another contributing factor, he added.

But he said that improving margins in Asia were already having a knock-on effect in the Mediterranean, where gross cash margins for a typical complex refiner have risen to around $2.40 per barrel, compared to a sickly $1.55 last year.
"We are already outperforming our expectations."
